articles.title: Russia Hacked Routers to Steal Microsoft Office Tokens
articles.summary: Microsoft's April Patch Tuesday served up a staggering 167 vulnerabilities including a SharePoint zero-day and Windows Defender's 'BlueHammer' flaw. Meanwhile, Chrome patched its fourth zero-day of the year because apparently nobody knows how to code anymore.

articles.title: Meta U-turns on encryption push for Instagram as DMs go plaintext
articles.summary: The 'Dirty Frag' Linux vulnerability gives instant root on all major distros with a public exploit and zero patches available. Some genius broke the disclosure embargo, leaving admins completely exposed to this root-level nightmare.

articles.title: GNU IFUNC is the real culprit behind CVE-2024-3094
articles.summary: CISA gave federal agencies exactly four days to patch an Ivanti EPMM zero-day being actively exploited in the wild. Because nothing says 'government efficiency' like discovering you're already pwned.

articles.title: Anti-DDoS Firm Heaped Attacks on Brazilian ISPs
articles.summary: Canvas got absolutely wrecked during finals week, disrupting education for millions of students nationwide. ShinyHunters defaced the login page with ransom demands because apparently even cybercriminals understand dramatic timing.

articles.title: Congress Narrowed the GUARD Act, But Serious Problems Remain
articles.summary: Russian military hackers mass-harvested Microsoft Office authentication tokens by exploiting ancient router vulnerabilities. Yet another reminder that your ancient Linksys is basically a welcome mat for state-sponsored spies.

articles.title: Canvas Got Hacked During Finals Week and Students Are Freaking Out
articles.summary: NVIDIA confirmed a GeForce NOW data breach affecting Armenian users after initially trying to stay quiet. Nothing says 'we take security seriously' like getting caught with your digital pants down.

articles.title: Big Finance Might Be Dooming the SPLC — Even Before Its Day in Court
articles.summary: The DOJ now treats dodging FOIA requests as a criminal offense punishable by arrest and strip searches. The irony of the most secretive administration in history criminalizing transparency evasion is absolutely chef's kiss.

articles.title: Hackers ate my homework: Educational SaaS Canvas down after cyberattack
articles.summary: Meta pulled a stunning U-turn on Instagram encryption, reverting DMs back to plaintext after years of privacy promises. Zuckerberg apparently decided he missed reading everyone's messages after all.

articles.title: Patch Tuesday, April 2026 Edition
articles.summary: Scattered Spider's 'Tylerb' pleaded guilty to wire fraud and identity theft for his role in the group's 2022 SMS phishing campaigns. Another legend falls to the feds, proving even the most elite social engineers eventually meet their match.

articles.title: U.S. Fuel Exports Hit Record High as Hormuz Crisis Reshapes Global Energy Flows
articles.summary: Researchers discovered 'Quasar Linux RAT' targeting developers to compromise software supply chains through credential harvesting and keylogging. Because apparently the easiest way to hack everyone is to hack the people who build everything first.
